verses.translation_literal: Of David. Do not fret yourself over the evildoers; do not be jealous of the doers of wrong.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of David, and it begins with a hand laid on a shoulder. Do not burn. Do not let your heart heat itself red over those who do harm. And do not look at the ones who work crooked things with that thin, sidelong hunger that is envy.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is not a rant against the wicked; it is a wise old man talking a younger one down from a ledge. Play it quiet and close. The speaker has seen exactly what the listener is seeing: thugs doing well.

The verb תִּתְחַר is the first problem. Rashi, Radak and Meiri link it to Jer 12:5 ('how will you compete with horses?'), so it means 'don't get tangled up with them, don't race them'. Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Malbim also hear חרה, 'to burn with anger'. The KJV's 'fret' picks the second and flattens the first. 'Fret' is a gentle, drawing-room word; in Hebrew the heat is real, and Malbim sees two separate temptations here: anger at their way, and the wish to be like them. The KJV's 'evildoers' and 'workers of iniquity' are fair; 'iniquity' is a heavy word for עַוְלָה, which is plainly 'crookedness, injustice'. The KJV also prints 'A Psalm of David' where the Hebrew has only the preposition לְ before David: 'of / to / for David', no more.

philological_notes.note: Either 'burn with anger' (Hithpael of חרה) or 'contend with, compete' as in Jer 12:5 'how will you compete (תְתַחֲרֶה) with horses'. Both senses suit the psalm: anger at the wicked and the urge to match them.
'Be jealous, envy'. Rashi takes it to the end point: do not envy them so far as to do wrong like them.

verses.translation_literal: For like the grass quickly they will be cut down, and like the green of new growth they will wither.
verses.translation_dramatic: For they are grass, and grass does not last. Soon the scythe, soon the sun, and they are cut. They are the first green of the field after the rains, so bright, and so quick to droop.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the speaker gives the reason for patience, and it is a farmer's reason. Palestinian grass springs green after the winter rain and is brown straw within weeks once the dry east wind (the sirocco) comes. Everyone in the room has watched it happen. The line is not a threat; it is a weather report.

The KJV's 'cut down' and 'wither' are right in sense; they translate two different verbs, ימלו (a cutting word, Rashi and Metzudat Zion) and יבולון (fading, rotting, Metzudat Zion). The KJV's 'they shall soon be cut down' puts the speed at the front, where the Hebrew puts it after 'like the grass': 'like grass, quickly'. And 'green herb' for יֶרֶק דֶּשֶׁא is a little dull: it is the newest green, the part that wilts first (Radak, Meiri).

philological_notes.note: A verb of cutting off (Rashi: 'cutting'; Metzudat Zion compares 'I will cut them off', Ps 118). Radak derives it from נמל and compares Job 18:16, 'his harvest is cut off'. The two readings agree: a clean cut, not slow decay.
Literally 'the green of new growth'. Radak and Meiri read it as the tender green part, which is the part that dries first while the root stays in the ground.

verses.translation_literal: Trust in YHWH and do good; dwell [in] the land and graze [on] faithfulness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lean on the LORD. Do good, and keep doing it. Settle in the land and stay there, quiet as a flock on a hillside, and feed on faithfulness, which does not run dry.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four commands, one after another, short as footsteps. Do not rush them: they are the opposite of 'fret'. The speaker moves from the heart (trust) to the hand (do good) to the home (dwell) to the table (graze).

The last clause is where the versions part. רְעֵה is the shepherd's verb: to graze, to tend. The KJV, 'verily thou shalt be fed', takes אֱמוּנָה as an adverb ('truly') and turns a command into a promise, and it also adds 'so shalt thou', which the Hebrew does not have. The Hebrew is four imperatives. Options for the last one: 'feed on faithfulness' (the reward of trusting God, Rashi), 'tend faithfulness' as a shepherd keeps a flock (Ibn Ezra compares 'a keeper of faithfulness'), or 'befriend'. All three keep the pastoral picture, which is exactly right for people whose wealth is sheep and fields. Radak adds that it also means teaching others in whatever place you live.

שְׁכָן־אֶרֶץ is 'dwell in the land': settle, take root, stop running after the wicked. In an agrarian world, being driven off the land is the great fear. The theme returns in vv. 9, 11.

philological_notes.note: 'Graze on / tend faithfulness'. The shepherd's verb, with 'faithfulness' as its object. Rashi: feed on the reward of the faith you kept; Ibn Ezra: like 'keeping faithfulness', since a shepherd is a keeper.
'Trust, rely, feel safe'. Radak calls trust the work of the heart, doing good the work of the hand, and teaching the work of the mouth.

verses.translation_literal: And take delight upon YHWH, and he will give you the requests of your heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: Make the LORD your delight, lean your whole soft weight on him as on a pillow, and he will answer what your heart has been asking.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb הִתְעַנֵּג is luxury, not duty: the root עֹנֶג is the soft, rich pleasure of a fine meal or a well-made bed. Rashi and Metzudat David take the preposition seriously: 'delight upon', as one reclines on a support (מִשְׁעֶנֶת). The KJV's 'delight thyself also in the Lord' adds 'also' that the Hebrew lacks and loses 'upon'.

The next phrase is easy to mishear as a blank cheque. מִשְׁאֲלוֹת is 'requests', things asked for, and the speaker has just said the one who delights in God will not ask for what the wicked have. Radak reads the command as a condition: if you take your delight in God, then what your heart asks will be what he gives. The imperative before 'and he will give' is a Hebrew way to say 'if you... then' (Radak, Meiri).

philological_notes.note: 'Take dainty pleasure upon'. Rashi and Metzudat David: luxuriate, as on the support of the LORD. The same verb returns in v. 11 for the humble delighting in peace.
'Requests, petitions', from שאל 'to ask'. Not 'desires' in the sense of cravings, as KJV has it.

verses.translation_literal: Roll upon YHWH your way, and trust upon him, and he will act.
verses.translation_dramatic: Roll your road onto the LORD, the way you roll a stone off your own back and onto stronger shoulders. Trust him. And he will act.
verses.directors_commentary:
גּוֹל is a physical word: roll, heave, shift a load. Rashi: 'roll all your needs onto him'; Ibn Ezra links it to 'cast your burden on the LORD' and reads 'way' as 'need'. Play it as relief: someone finally putting down a sack. The KJV's 'commit' is accurate in sense but turns a body-gesture into a legal word, and the load disappears.

Two short clauses end the verse: 'and he, he will act.' The pronoun is emphatic, after all the speaker's 'you' and 'your way'. The KJV's 'bring it to pass' supplies an object ('it') that the Hebrew leaves empty, and the emptiness is the point: the verb has no object because God's action is left open (Radak: he will do and complete everything). Leave the actor a silence.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of 'roll'. Rashi: 'roll all your needs on him'. Ibn Ezra explains the form as like סוב and compares 'cast your burden on the LORD'.
'Your way': road, course of life, and by extension your needs and plans. Ibn Ezra glosses it as 'your needs'.

verses.translation_literal: And he will bring out like the light your righteousness, and your justice like the noonday.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he will bring your righteousness out into the open, as dawn brings out the hills, and your cause will stand in full noon, with no shadow to hide in.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image is a courtroom made of weather. Someone has been slandered and kept in the dark; God brings the case out, first as light (the dawn), then as צָהֳרַיִם (noon). The noun is dual in form, 'double light', the sun at its height, the moment shadows disappear (Metzudat Zion: when the sun stands in the middle of the sky). Nothing at midday can be hidden, and that is the whole promise: not riches, but being seen as you are.

מִשְׁפָּט means both 'justice' and 'case, cause, verdict'; KJV 'judgment' is stiff and today reads as 'opinion'. The verb is the Hiphil of יצא, 'bring out', as one brings a prisoner or a verdict out. One verb governs both lines: the second 'your justice like the noonday' borrows 'he will bring out' from the first. Radak: all the world will know that your ways are in justice.

philological_notes.note: 'Noon', dual: the double light at the sun's height. Metzudat Zion links it to צוֹהַר, 'light, window'.
'Justice, verdict, rightful cause'. Here the vindication of the speaker's case in public.

verses.translation_literal: Be silent before YHWH and wait longingly [for] him; do not fret yourself over the one who makes his way prosper, over a man who does schemes.
verses.translation_dramatic: Be still before the LORD. Hush, and wait for him, and let the waiting be hard. Do not burn at the sight of the man whose road runs smooth, the man whose schemes all come off.
verses.directors_commentary:
דּוֹם is the first word to play: silence, the held breath. Rashi cites Jonathan's 'if they say, Wait (דֹּמּוּ) until we come to you' (1 Sam 14:9) and 'Aaron was silent' (Lev 10:3). The KJV's 'rest in the Lord' loses the silence; the Hebrew is the stillness of someone who has stopped arguing.

The second verb, הִתְחוֹלֵל, is split in the tradition. Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion hear 'hope, wait' (תּוֹחֶלֶת); Ibn Ezra, and Radak as an alternative, hear חיל, 'to writhe', like a woman in labour. Both are good theatre. The waiting is not calm: it hurts. The KJV's 'wait patiently' makes it gentler than either reading.

Then the repeated warning, 'do not fret', and now the target has a face: a man whose way succeeds, who 'does schemes'. מְזִמּוֹת can be plans without a moral tone, but here it carries the sense of plotting, since Ps 37:12 uses the verb זמם for the wicked. The KJV's 'wicked devices' adds 'wicked' to the noun.

philological_notes.note: 'Be silent, be still'. Rashi cites 1 Sam 14:9 and Lev 10:3; Rashi says it also means 'wait for his salvation'.
Either 'wait, hope' (from תוחלת, Rashi, Radak, Meiri) or 'writhe, as in labour' (from חיל, Ibn Ezra, and an alternative in Radak).
'Schemes, plots'. Closely tied to the verb זמם in v. 12.

verses.translation_literal: Let go of anger and forsake rage; do not fret yourself; only to do evil.
verses.translation_dramatic: Loosen your grip on anger. Walk away from rage. Do not let yourself burn. It goes one way only: toward doing evil yourself.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse has the shape of someone unclenching a fist. הֶרֶף is 'slacken, let drop' (Metzudat Zion links it to רפיון, slackness). 'Cease', the KJV's word, is the right drift but it sounds like an order from a magistrate; the Hebrew picture is a hand opening. 'Anger' and 'wrath' are two words for the same heat (Radak calls it a doubling). In Hebrew אַף is literally 'nose', the flared nostril.

The last clause is cut off, and each version fills the gap differently. The KJV's 'in any wise to do evil' makes 'only' into 'in any wise'; ASV 'it tendeth only to evil-doing' is closer. The Hebrew just says 'only to do evil' and lets the listener finish: the end of that road is doing harm yourself. Rashi: it brings God's wrath on you; Radak: do not join the evildoers because you see them prosper; Meiri: your anger will drive you to worse deeds. Play the clause as a stopped breath.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative: 'slacken, let go'. Metzudat Zion links it to רִפְיוֹן.
'Only to do evil': the sentence breaks off, and the tradition reads it as 'it leads only to evil (for you)'. Radak compares Num 14:9, 'only against the LORD do not rebel'.

verses.translation_literal: For evildoers will be cut off, and those who wait for YHWH, they will possess [the] land.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the doers of harm will be cut off, root and branch, and those who wait for the LORD, they, they, will take the land as their own.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker turns from advice to a promise, and the turn is built into the grammar: 'evildoers... will be cut off; and as for those who wait for the LORD, they'. The standalone pronoun הֵמָּה ('they') points a finger: not the others, those. The verb 'cut off' (כרת) is the covenant-cutting verb, and also the verb for cutting a tree. Ibn Ezra: it means their seed is cut off.

קוֹוֵי יְהוָה, 'those who wait for YHWH', has the same root as 'hope' (קוה, from a word for a stretched cord). KJV 'wait upon' sounds like waiting at table; ASV's 'wait for' is correct. The KJV's 'inherit the earth' for אֶרֶץ goes cosmic where the context (v. 3, 'dwell in the land') is the Land, the family plot; the KJV itself says 'land' in v. 3. 'Inherit' is also a little soft: יָרַשׁ is to take possession, to dispossess others (Malbim: they will inherit the cut-off evildoers).

philological_notes.note: 'They will be cut off', Niphal with the old -ון ending, a note of weight. Ibn Ezra: the sense is that their offspring are cut off.
'Those who wait with hope for'. Radak explains the spelling and compares Isa 40:31, 'those who wait for the LORD renew strength'.

verses.translation_literal: And yet a little, and there is no wicked [man]; and you will look closely upon his place, and he is not.
verses.translation_dramatic: Only a little longer, and the wicked man is not. Look for him. Stand where his house stood, look hard at the ground where he strutted, and he is not there.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the most visual verse so far, and it is a vanishing act. Do it in two beats: 'and he is not', and then, after the pause, the same words again. The Hebrew uses אֵין and אֵינֶנּוּ, 'there is no' and 'he is not', the language of a missing person, set against v. 7, where his 'way prospers': now he is gone.

הִתְבּוֹנַנְתָּ is not a glance: it is close, patient inspection, the verb of a surveyor or a judge. The KJV's 'diligently consider his place' puts the effort right, but 'consider' is mental; the Hebrew is looking at a spot of ground. Radak: you will search to see whether any root or stock remains of him, and find nothing. The KJV 'and it shall not be' also changes the subject: the Hebrew ends with the man, 'he is not' (ASV gets this right).

The KJV prints 'For yet a little while' where the Hebrew 'and yet a little' has just a 'vav' (and), no 'for'.

philological_notes.note: 'You will look closely, examine'. Radak: you will inspect to see whether a root or a stock of him is left, and find none.
'And he is not': the standard Hebrew for someone gone, dead or disappeared. Rashi: he has died and perished.

verses.translation_literal: And the humble will possess [the] land, and they will take delight upon the abundance of peace.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the humble, the bowed, the ones nobody noticed, they will take the land, and they will sit down in it, and feast on peace until it overflows.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker lets the weight of the whole psalm fall on one word: עֲנָוִים. These are not mild-mannered people. The word is related to עָנִי, 'poor, afflicted': the people pushed low, bent in front of those with power (Radak: those who were small before the wicked). Ibn Ezra reads the verse as an exact opposite of v. 9's evildoers.

Two things the KJV changes. First, 'meek' (also in Matthew 5:5, where this verse is echoed) is a passive, gentle word today; the Hebrew people are the lowly and oppressed who are finally lifted. Second, 'the earth': the Hebrew is the same אֶרֶץ as in vv. 3 and 9, 'the land', the family holding that can be taken away. And the verb of delight is the same עָנַג of v. 4: take your delight on the LORD, and then on the peace that follows. 'Abundance of peace' is רֹב שָׁלוֹם, a fullness of well-being, not merely the absence of war. Ibn Ezra: when the wicked are gone, the land has peace; Radak cites Prov 11:10, 'when the wicked perish there is rejoicing'.

philological_notes.note: 'The humble, the lowly'; kin to עָנִי 'afflicted'. Radak: those who were abased before the wicked.
'Peace, wholeness, well-being'. Meiri reads 'abundance of peace' as an allusion to lasting peace, citing Isa 60:21.

verses.translation_literal: The wicked [man] is plotting against the righteous, and gnashing at him his teeth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And still the wicked man schemes against the righteous. He sits and plans, and grinds his teeth at him, hard and slow.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm drops the comfort and shows the threat. The first line is silent work, the second noisy: the plotting is done at a desk, the grinding of teeth in the open. Both participles are present: the wicked man is doing this now, as the listener watches.

The verb זָמַם is the one behind v. 7's מְזִמּוֹת: it means to plan, scheme, devise (Metzudat Zion: thought). It is used for deliberate, planned harm. The KJV's 'plotteth' is right. Its 'gnasheth upon him with his teeth' adds 'with', which the Hebrew does not need: the teeth are the object, 'gnashing at him his teeth'. Rashi compares Lam 2:16, 'they gnash the teeth'. The gesture is in the Hebrew Bible a sign of hatred, or of frustrated malice, and an ancient audience would see it as a threat made with the body, face to face.

Meiri hears scorn in the gesture; Radak hears the moment of catching someone out, 'I found you!'; Ibn Ezra adds that the righteous man must hate him and keep away. The next verse (not in this window) answers with the LORD laughing: this verse is the threat it answers.

philological_notes.note: 'Plotting, devising'. Radak: 'thinking'; Metzudat Zion: 'an idea of thought'.
'Gnashing, grinding'. Rashi cites Lam 2:16, 'they gnash the teeth'. Metzudat Zion: the grinding of teeth in rage.

verses.translation_literal: My Lord laughs at him, for he has seen that his day comes.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the Lord laughs. Not the laughter of cruelty, but the quiet laughter of one who has already read the last page: he sees it coming, the day that belongs to that man, and it is on its way.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm turns from the scheming of the wicked to the one who watches them. The verb sachaq, 'laugh', is the same verb used of God's scorn for the kings of the earth in Psalm 2:4, and the effect is the same: the powerful are made small. Do not play it as a sneer. Ibn Ezra and Radak both read it as the laughter of knowledge: God knows how it ends.

The KJV 'shall laugh at him' reads as a prediction; the Hebrew imperfect is a present, ongoing laugh, and the two verbs that follow ('sees', 'comes') are what it rests on. 'His day' is a compressed phrase for the day of reckoning, whether death (Metzudat David) or punishment (Meiri). The title is 'adonay, 'my Lord', not the divine name, a rare note of personal address: the speaker's own master laughs.

philological_notes.note: To laugh, play or mock. With lamed ('laugh at him') it is derision. The imperfect describes what God is doing even now, while the plot proceeds.
'His day': a day that has been assigned to him, the day of his fall. The text does not say whether it is death or judgment.

verses.translation_literal: A sword the wicked have opened, and they have trodden their bow, to make fall the poor and needy, to slaughter the upright of way.
verses.translation_dramatic: Swords are bared; bows are bent under the foot. The wicked are armed and ready, and the targets they have chosen are the poor, the needy, the ones who walk straight, to be struck down and slaughtered.
verses.directors_commentary:
The wicked are armed, and the victims are named as the defenceless: 'ani, the poor, afflicted, and 'evyon, the needy. 'Opened a sword' is an odd phrase and the commentators split on it. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri give two readings: drawn from the sheath, as one opens a prisoner's cell, or sharpened, as in 'a sword is opened' (Ezek 21:33) and Psalm 55:22. Either way the action is deliberate.

'Trodden the bow' is what an archer does: he steps on the lower end of a bow to string it, a bit of concrete military detail the KJV's 'bent' passes over. The infinitives 'to make fall' and 'to slaughter' are blunt; tavach is the word for butchering animals (the KJV's 'slay' loses that). The victims are 'upright of way', not 'of upright conversation': the KJV uses 'conversation' in its archaic sense of 'conduct', which today's reader will misread as speech.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'opened'. Taken as 'drew out of its sheath' or 'sharpened'; the commentators do not agree.
To slaughter, the verb of the butcher and of sacrificial killing. It makes the victims livestock.

verses.translation_literal: Their sword will enter into their heart, and their bows will be broken.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the blade finds another road. It enters their own hearts, and the bows they bent snap in their hands.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reversal is the whole point. The weapons drawn in verse 14 come back on those who drew them; Radak points to Psalm 7:16, 'he falls into the pit he made'. 'Heart' is the centre of the person, not only the organ: the sword goes where the plan was made. The verb 'will be broken' is a passive plural-feminine ('bows' in Hebrew is feminine plural), and the fall is not attributed to any agent, leaving it to God.

The KJV 'shall enter' is accurate. The BBE's 'turned into' is an interpretation. Ibn Ezra notes the 'their' in 'their heart' points back to the wicked, not to the righteous.

philological_notes.note: 'in their own heart': the suffix 'their' refers to the wicked, who receive the blow.

verses.translation_literal: Good is little to the righteous, more than the wealth of many wicked.
verses.translation_dramatic: Better a little, held by honest hands, than the great heaps of wealth that many wicked men have gathered.
verses.directors_commentary:
A proverb in a psalm. 'Good is little to the righteous' leaves out 'is better', which English needs; Hebrew uses the comparative min, 'more than', to carry it. Radak reads hamon as 'wealth' (like mamon), supported by Ecclesiastes 5:9 ('who loves wealth'); the KJV's 'riches of many wicked' has it right. The word 'many' may attach to the wicked, to their wealth, or to the high-status people ('great ones', Radak, Metzudat Zion), so there is wordplay on rav as 'many' and 'great'.

Radak connects it to Proverbs 13:25: the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul, but the belly of the wicked lacks. The contrast to verse 14's 'poor and needy' is intentional: a poor righteous man is the better off.

philological_notes.note: Usually 'crowd, noise'. Here, as the commentators take it, 'wealth, abundance', like mamon.
'Many', or 'great ones': Radak notes Jeremiah 41:1 where the rabbim of the king are his nobles.

verses.translation_literal: For [the] arms of [the] wicked will be broken, and sustaining [the] righteous [is] YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their arms, those strong arms of the wicked, will snap, every one of them. But the righteous are not left to fall. Beneath them, bearing their weight, stands the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is built as a balance: two clauses, two kinds of people, two opposite fates, one for each arm-and-hand image. The wicked are named by their arms, the body part of strength, of the bow, the sword and the oppressor's grip. In a world where power is physical, to break the arm is to end the threat. The righteous have no arms mentioned at all; what they have is a supporter. Play the contrast: what breaks, and what holds.

The Hebrew saves the name for the very last word, so the sentence ends on YHWH like a door closing. The KJV ("but the Lord upholdeth the righteous") moves the divine subject to the front, rewrites the participle "sustaining" as a finite verb, and prints the name as "the Lord", which hides the personal name. The ASV restores "Jehovah" but keeps the same order. The participle סוֹמֵךְ is ongoing action: not a single rescue, but a continual propping. The verb is also the one used for laying a hand on a sacrificial animal (Lev 1:4), a physical image of leaning one's weight on something; the director may let the actor lean. Note too the plural verb form with feminine ending: "arms" is a feminine noun, and the verb agrees. Ibn Ezra hears the arms as those that bend the bows, so the two halves answer each other; Radak reads the verse as a promise that the wicked will have no power to harm the righteous, because God holds them up so they do not fall from fear of the wicked.

philological_notes.note: 'Arms', the limb of strength, a standard biblical image for power, military or otherwise. Here the arms are those of the wicked, and they are what breaks. Ibn Ezra specifies the arms that draw the bows.

A participle: 'and one who sustains', an ongoing action. The root means to lean on, support, lay a hand upon; the sense here is that YHWH is the standing support of the righteous. The participle has no 'shall' and no tense of its own, which the KJV's 'upholdeth' only partly keeps.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH is knowing the days of the blameless, and their inheritance for ever will be.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD knows the days of the blameless, every one, and what they are given will not pass away.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Knowing' in Hebrew is more than information: Radak compares 'the LORD knows the way of the righteous' (Ps 1:6), where yada' means he acknowledges and watches over them. 'Days' is the span of a life with its trials; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read 'how many years they will live', Rashi 'the deeds of their days'. 'Blameless' (tamim) is the word for an unblemished sacrificial animal, a whole, sound life; the KJV 'upright' blurs it with yashar in verse 14.

The 'inheritance' (nachalah) is the family land in the Israelite economy, which cannot be sold away permanently. 'For ever' may mean the world to come (Radak's father), or this world, as an inheritance passed to children (Ibn Ezra, per Radak). For a listener in a farming society it also means the land stays in the family.

philological_notes.note: Whole, complete, blameless; of sacrificial animals, without blemish.
Inheritance, a hereditary holding; the family land. Radak records two readings: the world to come, or the good this world passes to children.

verses.translation_literal: They will not be ashamed in a time of evil, and in days of famine they will be satisfied.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the evil time they will not be shamed. And when the days of famine come, they will eat and be filled.
verses.directors_commentary:
In a farming economy dependent on winter rain, famine is the great fear: the people hearing this know what a bad year does. The promise is not that evil times will not come but that the righteous will not be put to shame in them: shame here is the failure of one's expectation, being left standing with nothing when others looked on. Radak lists the 'evil time' as plague, war, or wild beasts; Malbim contrasts the wicked, who find no refuge.

The pair ra'ah (evil) and ra'avon (famine) sound alike; ra'avon is a rare form, which Radak compares to parzon. 'Be satisfied' (sava') is the same verb as in Proverbs 13:25 which Meiri quotes. The KJV 'ashamed' is fine; the BBE's 'when all are in need of food' paraphrases.

philological_notes.note: Famine, hunger; an unusual form (cf. Gen 42:33), which Radak notes follows the pattern of 'parzon'.

verses.translation_literal: For wicked men will perish, and the enemies of YHWH [will be] like the splendour of pastures; they have ended, in smoke they have ended.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the wicked will perish. The enemies of the LORD: like the glory of the green pastures, like the fat of the lambs: they vanish, and in smoke, in smoke, they vanish.
verses.directors_commentary:
The hardest line in this window. 'Like the yiqar of karim' can be read three ways, and Jewish tradition reads all three. Karim means 'lambs/rams' (plural, so KJV, Radak, Metzudat David: the fat of lambs, burned on the altar and going up in smoke) or 'pastures' (so Rashi and Ibn Ezra: grass or morning mist on a plain, which does not last). The consonants are the same. Yiqar is 'preciousness, splendour': either 'the glory of the meadows' or 'the best of the lambs', meaning the fat, the choicest part burned.

The repetition kalu ... kalu, 'they end, in smoke they end', is a refrain that acts like a drumbeat: the first for the splendour, the second for the wicked (Ibn Ezra). The KJV's 'consume away' hides the identical verb. Because it is the altar's smoke, there is bitter irony: those who killed the poor like animals go up like an offering.

philological_notes.note: 'Like the splendour of pastures' or 'like the fat of lambs'. Rashi gives both morning mist over a plain and fattened lambs; Radak and Metzudat David: fat burned on the altar.
To end, be finished off, be consumed. Said twice; the second is stressed on the first syllable at verse end, Ibn Ezra and Radak note.

verses.translation_literal: The wicked is borrowing and does not repay, and the righteous is showing favour and giving.
verses.translation_dramatic: The wicked man borrows and never pays it back. The righteous man is gracious, and gives.
verses.directors_commentary:
In an agrarian economy, loans were taken in bad years and a debtor who defaulted could ruin his lender, so a borrower who never repays is a man who treats other people's survival as his own purse. The wicked here is not a violent man but a defaulter. The righteous is the opposite: chonen, who shows favour (grace), and noten, who simply gives; the KJV 'sheweth mercy' softens a verb that is closer to 'is gracious'. Radak notes the double verb to stress giving again and again.

The verbs are participles in both halves: these are habits, not single acts. Rashi gives a reading where God is the righteous one, who gives to the creditor what the debtor took. Metzudat David has the righteous lender forgive the debt.

philological_notes.note: To show favour, be gracious, give unearned help. The root of chen, 'grace'.

verses.translation_literal: For his blessed ones will possess the land, and his cursed ones will be cut off.
verses.translation_dramatic: For those he has blessed will hold the land, and those he has cursed will be cut off from it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The land is the great promise of this psalm; 'inherit the land' (yirshu arets) recurs in verses 9, 11, 22, 29 and 34. Arets can mean 'earth' (KJV) or 'the land' of Israel; for an audience whose wealth is a plot of ground, the second is concrete. The 'his' is God: Radak, Rashi and Metzudat David read 'those blessed by him', not by the righteous man of verse 21.

'Cut off' (karat) is the vocabulary of covenant (a covenant is 'cut') and also of being removed from the community and the land. The pair blessed/cursed echoes Genesis 12:3 and Deuteronomy 28. The KJV 'such as be blessed of him' is archaic; 'of him' means 'by him'.

philological_notes.note: 'They will be cut off': removed from the land and from the people; the same verb is used for making a covenant.

verses.translation_literal: From YHWH the steps of a man are established, and his way he delights in.
verses.translation_dramatic: From the LORD come the steps of a man, firmly set; and the LORD takes delight in his way.
verses.directors_commentary:
Gever is the strong man, the one who is on his feet (Rashi reads 'a man mighty in the fear of God'; Meiri, one who strives to get through his lean days). 'Steps' (mitsadei) are the individual strides, set apart from 'way' (derekh), the road as a whole: the line says God fixes both the stride and the road, as Malbim points out. 'Established' (konenu) is a passive that means 'set firm, prepared'.

The KJV 'good man' adds 'good' (only the Webster marks it in brackets); the Hebrew just says gever, 'man', and the goodness is from context. Whose delight is it? Most read that God delights in the man's way (Radak, Metzudat David); YLT has the man delighting in it. I follow the first.

philological_notes.note: Steps, strides; Metzudat Zion glosses 'his steps'.
Passive: set firm, made ready. The same root builds 'kavanah' and 'prepared'.

verses.translation_literal: Though he falls, he will not be hurled down, for YHWH is supporting his hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: He may fall, but he will not lie flung on the ground. For the LORD has taken his hand and holds it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture is a father with a child learning to walk: the hand is gripped. Ki yippol means 'if he falls', not 'when'; Rashi glosses the particle as 'if'. The verb yutal (Hophal of tul) is 'be hurled, flung' as in Jonah 1:12, and the KJV's 'utterly' translates nothing: the Hebrew says 'he will not be thrown', and Radak, Metzudat David and Rashi explain it as 'not thrown completely to the ground', i.e. not abandoned.

Radak sets the fall into the pattern of Proverbs 24:16, 'seven times a righteous man falls and rises'. The hardship that causes the fall is a form of God's correction, he says, as in Proverbs 3:12. Sound to hear: yippol (falls) and yutal (hurled) share their final l, and the verse closes on 'his hand'.

philological_notes.note: Hophal: to be hurled, flung down. Rashi: 'not thrown away to be forsaken'.

verses.translation_literal: A lad I was, also I have grown old, and I have not seen a righteous one forsaken, and his seed seeking bread.
verses.translation_dramatic: I was a boy once. Now my beard is white. And in all those years, through every season of the road, I have not once seen the righteous man left alone in the dust, nor his children out among the doorways, hunting for a crust.
verses.directors_commentary:
An old man speaks, and everything in the verse depends on his age: it is testimony from a long life, not a theory. Play it slowly, with the weight of someone who has watched many families rise and fall. Bread is the whole of the ancient household economy; a family with no grain in the jar and no land to fall back on had only the kindness of neighbours, so 'his seed seeking bread' means the worst thing the village could picture, descendants reduced to asking at doors.

The KJV 'now am old' adds a 'now' the Hebrew does not have: it says 'also I have grown old', two plain facts side by side. KJV 'begging bread' makes the children beggars, but the Hebrew is the neutral 'seeking', the very verb used in v. 32 for the wicked 'seeking' to kill. Radak and Meiri both hear a limit in the claim: the righteous may be poor, but not utterly forsaken. Rashi, quoted from the Talmud, even says David was not old enough for the line, so he hears the voice of the 'Prince of the World' speaking through it.

philological_notes.note: 'Forsaken' or 'abandoned'. The same root returns in v. 28 ('he will not abandon') and v. 33 ('he will not abandon him in his hand'), so the verse opens the chapter's argument: the one who is not forsaken is held by God. Radak glosses it as lacking bread and clothing, citing Jacob's prayer at Genesis 28:20.

Literally 'his seed'. The word carries the whole generational frame of the psalm: the righteous have seed that is blessed (v. 26), the wicked have seed that is cut off (v. 28). Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as the young children left behind.

verses.translation_literal: All the day [he is] showing favour and lending, and his seed [is] for a blessing.
verses.translation_dramatic: Every day the same: his hand open, his purse open, giving where there is need and lending where there is lack. And the children that come after him go out into the world as a blessing.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture of the righteous man is now concrete: he is the one who has something and shares it. In a peasant economy a loan to a neighbour was often how a family got through a bad harvest, and Israelite law (Deut 15) pushes the lender to lend freely and not to charge interest, so 'lending' here is generosity, not business. The two participles, 'showing favour' and 'lending', are ongoing: this is what he does all day long, as a habit, not an occasional gift.

The KJV 'his seed is blessed' turns the Hebrew's 'for a blessing' into a passive state, something done to them. The Hebrew says they are a blessing (compare Genesis 12:2), the source of good for others. Rashi and Radak both read it that way, and Radak also offers the other reading, that people will bless them when they see them. 'All the day' is an idiom for 'continually', as Radak notes with Psalm 25:5.

philological_notes.note: 'For a blessing': a lamed of result, 'become a blessing'. Not 'blessed' (KJV), which would need a passive participle such as בָּרוּךְ. Radak compares Genesis 12:2 ('be a blessing').
Idiom for 'continually, all the time', not strictly 'all day long'.

verses.translation_literal: Turn aside from evil and do good, and dwell for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: Turn from evil. Do good. And stay: stay on the ground that is yours, for good.
verses.directors_commentary:
After testimony comes the command, three short imperatives in a row, the bare rhythm of a teacher's voice. Speak it flatly and quickly, almost like a proverb. The last imperative is the surprise: 'dwell' is the reward, not another duty. Ibn Ezra notes that it stands for a future ('you will dwell'), as with 'go up and die' in Deuteronomy 32:49–50. Meiri takes it the same way.

The KJV 'depart from evil' is fine, though archaic; 'dwell for evermore' makes the Hebrew sound like heaven, while the verb שָׁכַן is about living settled in the land, and Radak hears it as 'dwelling securely'. Both Ibn Ezra and Radak read the two halves as the prohibitions and the commands of the law, 'turn from evil' and 'do good', and Radak adds that turning from evil alone is not enough.

philological_notes.note: An imperative that works as a promise, 'and you will dwell'. The verb is settled residence, the opposite of wandering; Radak glosses it 'dwell securely'.
'Turn aside from evil'; the same expression as in Psalm 34:15, and a stock formula of the wisdom writers. Ibn Ezra reads it as the prohibitions and 'do good' as the positive commands.

verses.translation_literal: For YHWH [is] a lover of justice, and he will not abandon his devoted ones; for ever they are kept, but the seed of the wicked is cut off.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD loves justice. He does not leave his faithful ones behind: they are guarded, for ever guarded. But the seed of the wicked, like a branch under the blade, is cut away.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the reason for everything said so far, and it opens with 'for'. The verse sets two outcomes against each other with two verbs from the vocabulary of farming and guarding, 'kept' against 'cut off'. Play the second half harder, with a drop in the voice.

Two words repay attention. מִשְׁפָּט is more than the KJV's 'judgment': it is the act of setting things right, justice in the courtroom and in the world, and Radak ties it to 'the work of uprightness'. חֲסִידָיו, 'his devoted ones', is the KJV's 'saints', which makes them a holy class. The Hebrew חָסִיד is someone who practises חֶסֶד, loyal, covenant kindness. Radak notes the order: justice first, then chesed, because chesed goes beyond what the law requires. The verb 'cut off' (כרת) is the covenant and the farmer's verb: it is used for cutting a covenant and for cutting a branch. The verse leaves its ayin-line, 'for ever they are kept', as a short phrase in the middle with no stated subject, and Ibn Ezra reads 'they' as the righteous man and his children together.

philological_notes.note: 'His devoted ones', people who practise loyal kindness. Radak argues that chesed goes beyond the strict line of justice, which is why it comes right after 'justice'.
'Cut off'. Radak points out that 'seed' is named because with the wicked person his offspring are cut off too.

verses.translation_literal: Righteous ones will possess [the] land, and they will dwell for ever upon it.
verses.translation_dramatic: The righteous will take hold of the land, and they will settle on it, and they will never be moved from it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The land is the heart of the psalm, here said for the plain, steady third time. For an ancient Israelite family the land was the family's life: the field that fed them and the plot where their ancestors lay. 'Inherit' is the same verb as 'possess'; the KJV's 'inherit' makes it a gift from a father, while יָרַשׁ has the sense of taking possession, often even by force, as in the conquest.

The KJV 'dwell therein' is correct but stiff, and loses the closing 'upon it', the last word in the Hebrew, which seals the verse like a stone on a boundary. Radak notes the repetition ('possess' and 'dwell') as a deliberate doubling for strength, and Meiri likewise: the verse says the same thing twice so that no one doubts it.

philological_notes.note: 'Will possess'. The verb is about taking possession, not only receiving an inheritance; it is the standard word for Israel's taking of the land. It returns in v. 34 as 'to possess the land'.

verses.translation_literal: [The] mouth of [the] righteous utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice.
verses.translation_dramatic: Listen to the mouth of the righteous man: it murmurs wisdom. And his tongue speaks what is just.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the land to the voice. The verse is built as a pair: mouth and tongue, wisdom and justice. In a world where almost no one read, the righteous man was known by what he said at the gate, where disputes were settled and the elders sat. Say it quietly, as if turning a phrase over.

The verb יֶהְגֶּה is the key word and the KJV's 'speaketh' is too weak. It means to murmur, mutter or meditate aloud, the sound of someone repeating words under their breath, as in Psalm 1:2, where the blessed man 'meditates' on the law. Rashi reads it that way: first wisdom in the heart, then the tongue speaks justice. Metzudat Zion simply glosses it as 'speaks'. The second verb is the ordinary 'speak', so the Hebrew moves from the inner murmur to the spoken word. The KJV 'talketh of judgment' has the same flatness.

philological_notes.note: To murmur or meditate aloud: low, repeated speech, the sound of someone rehearsing words. The same verb is used for the man of Psalm 1:2 who meditates on the law. Rashi reads it as wisdom first in the heart, then spoken; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'speaks'.

verses.translation_literal: [The] law of his God [is] in his heart; his steps do not slip.
verses.translation_dramatic: The teaching of his God is in his heart, and so his feet keep their ground: his steps do not slide.
verses.directors_commentary:
The inside of the righteous man: the 'law' is in his heart, not on a scroll. In Hebrew the heart is the seat of thought and will, so it means he has it by memory and by choice. Radak hears 'his inside is like his outside': what the mouth of v. 30 speaks, the heart already holds. The echo of Deuteronomy 6:6 and Jeremiah 31:33 is clear.

The KJV 'none of his steps shall slide' turns a plain statement into a promise about 'none'. The Hebrew says 'his steps do not slip', and the verb תִמְעַד is singular and feminine, going with a feminine subject: the steps are many, but the slipping is treated one by one. Radak and Meiri pick up exactly this: not even one of his steps slips. The word אֲשֻׁרָיו, 'his steps', is rare and poetic; Rashi and Metzudat Zion both gloss it by 'feet' or 'steps'. Play it as the end of a thought, a man walking on a slippery path who does not fall.

philological_notes.note: 'Slips', 'totters': the loss of footing on a slippery or uneven path. Used again of the righteous man's feet in Psalm 18:37. Metzudat Zion glosses it as slipping.
'His steps': a rare poetic plural. Radak glosses it 'his feet'; Meiri notes the verb is singular, so 'not one of his steps' slips.

verses.translation_literal: [One] watching, a wicked [man], for the righteous [one], and seeking to kill him.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the wicked man is watching. He waits, eyes fixed on the righteous, and he is looking for the chance to kill him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns. After the quiet of the previous verse the threat enters, and the shift should be felt in the voice. The Hebrew begins with the participle, 'watching', and only then names the watcher, so the audience feels the stare before they know whose it is. The wicked man is not passing by; he is on the lookout, like a sentinel or a hunter at a path.

The verb צוֹפֶה is the word for a watchman on the wall, and that is what the KJV 'watcheth' flattens. The root בקש, 'seek', returns from v. 25, but now it seeks death, not bread. Ibn Ezra and Radak both read the motive as envy: the wicked man sees the righteous one doing well, and especially if his own fortunes fall, he looks for a way to bring him down. Radak sees a courtroom, a false accusation before the ruler.

philological_notes.note: 'Watching', 'keeping watch': the word for a sentinel (compare Ezekiel 33:6). The sense is of lying in wait, not a casual glance. Metzudat David glosses it 'looks in order to ambush'.
'And seeking'. The same root as 'seeking bread' in v. 25, now turned to a darker object.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH will not abandon him in his hand, and will not declare him guilty in his being judged.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the LORD will not walk away. He will not leave the righteous man in that hand, and when the day comes and the man is brought to judgment, the LORD will not let the verdict fall against him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse answers verse 32 directly: the wicked man lies in wait, and God does not hand his servant over. "In his hand" is the hand of the wicked, a grip from which the righteous cannot free himself. The second line moves from ambush to courtroom. In the ancient Near East a poor man's case was heard at the city gate before elders or a magistrate, and a powerful accuser could bring false charges, bribe witnesses or press a debt claim. The psalmist's promise is that the trial will not end in a guilty verdict.

The verb yarshi'enu is the Hiphil of rasha', "to declare guilty" or "to pronounce wicked", the legal opposite of declaring someone righteous (tsaddiq). The word play is deliberate: the wicked (rasha') of verse 32 will not succeed in having the righteous declared rasha'. The KJV's "leave him in his hand" and "condemn him when he is judged" are sound, though "leave" is a little weak for 'azav, which means abandon or forsake, the same verb as in verse 25. The KJV also renders the Niphal infinitive "when he is judged" correctly. The BBE's "into their hands" turns a singular hand into a plural.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of rasha', a forensic verb: to declare someone in the wrong, to find guilty. It is the counterpart of hitsdiq, to acquit. The verse says God will not let the court pronounce the righteous man guilty.
Niphal infinitive construct with suffix: 'when he is put on trial', literally 'in his being judged'. The Niphal is passive or reflexive, and it casts the righteous man as the defendant.

verses.translation_literal: Hope to YHWH and keep his way, and he will lift you high to possess [the] land; when the wicked are cut off, you will see.
verses.translation_dramatic: So wait. Wait for the LORD, and keep to his road. He will lift you up to take hold of the land, and on the day the wicked are cut away, you will be there to see it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm returns to its main command, the same as in v. 9 and at the start of the chapter: wait. The verb קוה means to wait with tension, hoping, stretched toward something, and is related to the word for a cord, so waiting here is an active leaning forward, not passive sitting. The KJV 'wait on' is old English for 'wait for', and the Hebrew has 'to' (אֶל), which makes it sound like waiting at table. 'Keep his way' is the other half: while you wait, you keep walking in it.

The promise has the verbs of v. 29 again: 'lift you high' and 'possess the land'. The KJV ends with 'thou shalt see it' and adds 'it' in italics; the Hebrew simply says 'you will see', leaving the object open, a strong, bare close. Ibn Ezra and Radak both hear the older generation speaking: 'I have seen it, so listen to me.' Malbim reads the 'land' as another, eternal land beyond this world, a reading found in later tradition and not required by the Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: 'Hope', 'wait expectantly'. Pi'el imperative, with the sense of straining toward something, and linked to the rope (קַו) image. The 'to' (אֶל) shows who is waited for.
'And he will lift you high' (the Polel of 'to be high'); the opposite of the lowness of the one the wicked tried to cast down. Meiri reads it as 'if you are low, he will raise you'.

token_glosses.gloss: and he will lift you high

verses.translation_literal: I have seen a wicked [man], ruthless, and spreading himself like a native [tree], luxuriant.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have seen it myself: a wicked man, feared, enormous, spreading out his branches like an old tree in its own soil, thick with green.
verses.directors_commentary:
The old man is back, with his own eyes: 'I have seen', the same verb as in v. 25, now for the other side of the account. He does not deny that the wicked prosper; he has seen them at their greatest. Let the voice swell here, almost in admiration, because the next verse will take it all away.

The picture is a tree, and the KJV 'green bay tree' is a famous mistake of the older translations: the Hebrew has no 'bay' and no named tree. אֶזְרָח is 'native', the word for the citizen born in the land (Leviticus 24:16), set against the 'sojourner' (גֵּר). A tree 'native' to its soil is one that grew where it was planted and is deep-rooted. Metzudat Zion and Radak understand it just that way, and Ibn Ezra and Meiri take it as a man with a large family. Rashi gives both readings: rooted in the land and full of possessions. The Hebrew is deliberately open between 'tree' and 'native man', and the English must choose. The word עָרִיץ is 'ruthless, one who inspires terror', not 'in great power' (KJV): he is the strong man that others fear. The verb מִתְעָרֶה is also uncertain: 'spreading' or 'stripping bare' or 'rooting', and Rashi and Metzudat Zion say 'rooting', as in Isaiah 19:7.

philological_notes.note: 'Native', the person born in the land, opposed to the גֵּר, the resident alien (Lev 24:16). The Hebrew has no tree name; Metzudat Zion says it means a tree planted long ago, and Rashi a rooted man full of possessions. 'Bay tree' of the KJV is a guess from the older versions.
Rare: 'spreading himself out' or 'baring himself', or 'rooting' (Rashi compares Isaiah 19:7). Ibn Ezra reads it as acting openly, in public, with every kind of evil.
'Ruthless', 'terrifying': the strong man who causes fear. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'strong'.
'Luxuriant', 'fresh, juicy': a tree that is wet and green. Metzudat Zion compares Jeremiah 17:8.

verses.translation_literal: And he passed, and look, he [is] not; and I sought him, and he was not found.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then he was gone. I looked, and there was nothing there. I searched for him, and he was not to be found.
verses.directors_commentary:
The great reversal, and the shortest verse of the window: all the weight of v. 35 is gone in six words. Play it in a hush, with a long pause after 'look'. The Hebrew is as bare as a tombstone: 'passed', 'look', 'not', 'sought', 'not found'. הִנֵּה, 'look!', is the word of sudden sight, and here the audience is made to look at an empty place.

Two word-plays make it ring. The wicked man who 'sought' the righteous man's death (v. 32) is now himself 'sought' and not found, the same root בקש. And אֵינֶנּוּ, 'he is not', is the language of death (compare Genesis 5:24 and 42:13). The KJV 'yet he passed away' adds 'yet' and 'away', which softens the sudden turn; the Hebrew has only 'and he passed'. Radak says even his place could not be found, so completely was he and his offspring finished. Malbim reads the search as a search in the world to come.

There is a textual wrinkle: the Hebrew has 'he passed' but 'I sought', switching person, and several ancient versions seem to read 'I passed by', which would make the speaker walk past the place and find the tree gone.

philological_notes.note: 'He is not': the Hebrew idiom for disappearance or death (compare Genesis 5:24, 'and he was not'). The shortest possible statement of the end of the wicked man.
'And I sought him': the same root that the wicked used to 'seek' the righteous man's death in v. 32 and the children 'seek' bread in v. 25. Now the seeker finds nothing.

verses.translation_literal: Guard the blameless and see the upright, for [there is] a future for a man of peace.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look closely at the blameless one. Take the measure of the upright. Watch how it ends for them, and you will find the ending is peace.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hinge of the psalm. For thirty-six verses the speaker has told us not to fret over the wicked who flourish; now he says: look at the whole life, not the good season. The verb 'shamar' is the shepherd's and the watchman's word, to guard, keep, observe, and the first thing the actor must do is look hard. The KJV 'mark the perfect man' is archaic: 'mark' means 'take note of', and 'perfect' misleads, because 'tam' is wholeness, a person with nothing held back or doubled. The ASV and the Hebrew read differently here: the Hebrew says 'there is an acharit to a man of shalom', not 'a happy end to the man of peace'. The KJV 'end of that man' also inserts 'that', which the Hebrew does not have. 'Acharit' is 'what comes after', and can mean both final outcome and the future that remains, as in the Targum's 'sof', end. Rashi on Psalms 37:37 reads it as a promise that if such a person has no beginning (no early success) he still has an afterwards.

philological_notes.note: 'What comes after': an outcome, an end, and a future. It is the psalm's key word, and it recurs in v. 38 for the wicked, where it is 'cut off'. English 'end' loses the hope in it.
'Whole, complete, blameless': the person whose conduct and speech match. 'Perfect' suggests sinlessness, which is not what the word says.

verses.translation_literal: And transgressors are destroyed together; the future of the wicked is cut off.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the rebels, the breakers of the line: together they are swept away. And the wicked, the afterward they counted on: it is cut off.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is built as a mirror to the last. 'Acharit' returns, but now with a verb of the axe: 'nikhratah', cut off, the same verb used of cutting a covenant and felling a tree. The wicked had a future in their own eyes, and the psalm takes it away in a single word. Ibn Ezra on Psalms 37:38 points out the pairing: 'transgressors' answer 'the blameless', and 'the wicked' answer 'the upright'. The KJV 'shall be destroyed' and 'shall be cut off' turn the verbs into future threats; the Hebrew perfect states what is already true, as an observed pattern, which is why the speaker can tell the listener to look. The KJV 'transgressors' is fair, since 'poshe'im' are those who rebel, not those who merely stumble. 'Yachdav', together, carries a note of collective doom: not one escapes, and they fall as they stood, in a crowd. The BBE 'cut off' for the first verb and 'destruction' for the second reverses the Hebrew and loses the axe image.

philological_notes.note: A strong verb of extermination, reserved for the complete removal of a people or house. It is the root of the later Hebrew word for forced apostasy, 'shemad'.
'It is cut off': the same root as 'to cut a covenant'. The fate here is the opposite: a line that is severed.

verses.translation_literal: And the salvation of the righteous [is] from YHWH, their stronghold in a time of trouble.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the rescue of the righteous does not come from them. It comes from the LORD, who is their fortress when the trouble comes.
verses.directors_commentary: The preposition is the whole point: 'me-YHWH', from YHWH. The righteous do not save themselves by their blamelessness; they are saved from outside, and the verse says so against the verses before it that might sound like a doctrine of reward. The KJV 'is of the Lord' is a seventeenth-century 'of', meaning 'from', and a modern reader hears 'belongs to', so it should be said 'from'. 'Ma'oz' is a mountain fortress, a place one climbs to when the plain is overrun; the KJV 'strength' loses the architecture. 'Et tzarah', a time of trouble, is a narrow place: the word 'tzarah' is related to 'tzar', tight, so trouble is being squeezed, and the stronghold is where there is room. Ibn Ezra on Psalms 37:39 compares the image of a strong tower elsewhere in Scripture. Radak on Psalms 37:39 notes the spelling of 'ma'uzzam' with a dagesh in the zayin, which makes the word 'their stronghold' and not a verb.

philological_notes.note: 'Their stronghold': a fortified place to which one flees, from the root of strength. Radak notes the dagesh in the zayin, marking the noun with its suffix.
'Trouble, distress': from the root 'to be narrow or bound'. It is the picture of being pressed in, which makes the stronghold a place of space.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH helped them, and delivered them; he delivers them from the wicked, and saves them, for they took refuge in him.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD helped them. He lifted them out. He lifts them out still, out of the hands of the wicked, and he saves them. And why? Because they ran to him and hid.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm closes on a pile of verbs, and the actor should let them stack: help, deliver, deliver, save. The Hebrew does not reduce them. It even doubles 'delivered' and 'delivers', first in a narrative form and then in a habitual one, so that the past rescue and the present one are heard side by side. Ibn Ezra on Psalms 37:40 reads the past as evidence: we have seen him deliver many, so he will deliver them always. Radak on Psalms 37:40 says the doubling expresses abundance of help, and adds the purpose of the whole psalm: to keep a person from being lured by the success of the wicked and doing as they do. The KJV 'because they trust in him' flattens 'chasu', which is to take shelter, as a bird or a fugitive hides under a rock or wing; trust is what this does, but the picture is a person running to cover. The KJV also turns the past 'they took refuge' into a present, and the BBE into a pluperfect, 'they had faith'. The last word, 'vo', in him, is the destination of the running, and it closes the verse and the section.

philological_notes.note: 'To take refuge, to shelter in': the image of a person under a rock or a wing. It is more bodily than 'trust'.
The same verb twice, once as narrative and once as habitual. 'Palat' is to slip someone out of a tight place, to bring them through to safety.
